title: 1 Samuel 19:1–7
context: In 1 Samuel 19 Saul’s jealousy of David turns into open intent to kill. Jonathan, who has already made a covenant of friendship with David (18:1–4), warns him, then speaks to Saul on David’s behalf, reminding his father of David’s service and the LORD’s victory over the Philistines. Saul swears not to kill David, and David is restored to court. Arminian and Reformed readers share the passage as a picture of courageous friendship, peacemaking, and God’s protection of his anointed.

verses.text: Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul’s son, greatly delighted in David.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul tells Jonathan and his servants to kill David, but Jonathan delights in David. Saul’s hostility is now open.

Arminian readers see Jonathan choosing loyalty to what is right over loyalty to his father’s command. His friendship, begun in 18:1–4, is now tested.
verses.reformedNotes:
Saul’s jealousy has hardened into a plan to kill. Jonathan’s love for David stands against it.

Reformed readers see God protecting his anointed through a friend placed in Saul’s own household. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Jonathan told David, saying, “Saul my father seeks to kill you. Now therefore, please take care of yourself in the morning, live in a secret place, and hide yourself.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan warns David that Saul seeks to kill him and tells him to hide in a secret place until morning. Friendship becomes protection.

Arminian readers see courageous kindness that risks the king’s displeasure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan acts quickly and practically. He keeps David informed and safe.

Reformed readers see God’s providence working through Jonathan’s faithful love. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about friendship that protects the innocent, even at personal cost to the one who shows it.

verses.text: I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will talk with my father about you; and if I see anything, I will tell you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan plans to stand with his father in the field near David’s hiding place and speak to Saul about him. He will report what he learns.

Arminian readers see a peacemaker seeking to change his father’s mind through honest appeal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan chooses to intercede before resorting to anything else. He positions David to hear the outcome.

Reformed readers see wise advocacy on behalf of the innocent. Both traditions read this as shared ground, admiring Jonathan’s careful courage in standing between his father and his friend.

verses.text: Jonathan spoke good of David to Saul his father, and said to him, “Don’t let the king sin against his servant, against David; because he has not sinned against you, and because his works have been very good toward you;
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan speaks well of David, urging Saul not to sin against an innocent servant whose deeds have benefited him. He names the act as sin.

Arminian readers see moral clarity combined with respect. Jonathan appeals to Saul’s conscience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan’s argument is simple: David has done nothing wrong and much good. Killing him would be sin.

Reformed readers see faithful rebuke offered to a king. Both traditions read this as shared ground about speaking truth to power with honor and courage.

verses.text: for he put his life in his hand and struck the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great victory for all Israel. You saw it and rejoiced. Why then will you sin against innocent blood, to kill David without a cause?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan reminds Saul that David risked his life against the Philistine and that the LORD gave Israel a great victory, which Saul saw and celebrated. Shedding innocent blood would be sin.

Arminian readers see an appeal to memory and gratitude.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan credits the victory over Goliath to the LORD (1 Samuel 17). David was God’s instrument.

Reformed readers see Jonathan recognizing God’s hand in David’s deeds. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting the seriousness of shedding innocent blood (compare Deuteronomy 19:10).

verses.text: Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan; and Saul swore, “As the LORD lives, he shall not be put to death.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul listens and swears, “As the LORD lives, he shall not be put to death.” For a moment he relents.

Arminian readers see that Saul could respond to good counsel. His later choices make the oath tragically empty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Saul’s oath is sincere in the moment. It will not hold.

Reformed readers see how unstable a heart can be when it is not settled in obedience. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note how quickly the reconciliation collapses in verses 9–10.

verses.text: Jonathan called David, and Jonathan showed him all those things. Then Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he was in his presence as before.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan reports everything to David and brings him back into Saul’s presence as before. Reconciliation seems complete.

Arminian readers see a peacemaker’s success, however brief. Jonathan’s efforts restore David to court.
verses.reformedNotes:
David returns to serve Saul. The restoration rests on Saul’s oath.

Reformed readers see a genuine but fragile peace. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the value of reconciliation, even when it proves temporary, and honor Jonathan’s role as mediator between his father and his friend.
